meta.title: Who really said "There's a Sucker Born Every Minute"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Artemus Ward never wrote it. The phrase was anonymous gamblers' slang in print by 1879; the credit to Ward first appears in 1888, 21 years after his death.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There's a Sucker Born Every Minute'?
meta.ogDescription: Anonymous swindlers' slang, in print by 1879. The Artemus Ward credit surfaces in 1888, 21 years after he died. And Barnum didn't say it either.

answer.label: Not Artemus Ward — an anonymous swindlers’ adage
answer.sourceLine: The line is the youngest member of a family of anonymous sayings that ran through nineteenth-century print — “a fool born every minute” (1806), “a flat born every minute” (1835) — before the ‘sucker’ wording surfaced, credited to nobody, in a Chicago newspaper on 2 January 1879. The first known credit to Artemus Ward is a small-town New York weekly of 6 October 1888, twenty-one years after his death, and the phrase appears nowhere in his collected works.

source.heading: Where the line actually shows up

docMeta.dd: An anonymous “old-timer” — the saying already sits inside quotation marks
“Geneseo Suckers,” The Nunda News (Nunda, New York), 6 October 1888 — twenty-one years after Ward’s death

source.excerpt: … in the season they make a bit on base ball, or on the races, and then, you know, ‘there’s a sucker born every minute,’ and rigid city legislation drives the hard-up gambler, who would be a decent one of the kind, to turn skin-dealer and sure-thing player.
trail: The saying has a long anonymous pedigree. Quote Investigator ↗ traces it from “that there vash von fool born every minute” in The European Magazine and London Review of January 1806, through “there is a flat born every minute” in Bell’s Life in London in 1835, to the first ‘sucker’ instance in The Inter-Ocean of 2 January 1879 — every one of them unattributed.

The Artemus Ward credit is dated and traceable. QI ↗ found it in “Geneseo Suckers,” The Nunda News of 6 October 1888, which closes a report on a jewellery swindle by telling the victims to console themselves with “that famous expression of Artemus Ward’s that ‘there is a sucker born every minute.’” Ward had been dead since March 1867.

Ward’s own writing does not contain it. A full-text search of The Complete Works of Artemus Ward ↗ — the seven-part collected edition, essays through the Panorama — returns no instance of “sucker,” “born every minute” or “fool born.” Neither does Don C. Seitz’s 1919 biography and bibliography ↗ of him.

Barnum inherited the line last, not first. QI’s earliest Barnum linkage ↗ is an October 1890 Chicago clothing-store advertisement using the word “fool”; the ‘sucker’ wording was not attached to him until a July 1892 newspaper item, after his death in 1891.
source.excerptNote: Transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗ from The Inter-Ocean of 2 January 1879. The single quotation marks around the saying are the newspaper’s own — a sign it was already circulating as gamblers’ slang, with no author attached to it.

source.rightsNote: Every documented appearance of this saying is a nineteenth-century one — 1806 through 1892 — and all of it is long out of copyright in the United States. There is also no author to hold rights in it: the phrase entered print as anonymous gamblers’ slang, and the newspapers that carried it were quoting a proverb, not coining a line.

author.name: Artemus Ward
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: Artemus Ward
author.metaLine: 1834–1867 · American humorist and lecturer, pen name of Charles Farrar Browne
author.bio: Charles Farrar Browne (1834–1867) wrote and performed as Artemus Ward, the deadpan travelling-showman persona whose misspelled letters and sold-out lectures made him one of the most popular American humorists of the 1860s. He befriended Mark Twain in Virginia City, Nevada, and recommended him to New York editors. Browne moved to England in 1866 and died of tuberculosis at Southampton on 6 March 1867; his remains were returned to Waterford, Maine the following year. Every book bearing his name was published in his lifetime or shortly after — and none of them contains this sentence.

misattribution.heading: Five owners, none of them the author
misattribution.intro: This line keeps changing hands. Quote Investigator’s chronology shows it passing from anonymous swindlers to a series of famous names — not one of whom can be shown to have coined it.

items.why: Browne died on 6 March 1867. The first known ascription to him comes twenty-one years later, in a jewellery-swindle report in The Nunda News of 6 October 1888 ↗, which tells the victims they can console themselves with “that famous expression of Artemus Ward’s.” The phrase is in none of his books.

Quote Investigator ↗ found no persuasive evidence Barnum spoke or wrote it: the earliest link is an October 1890 Chicago clothing-store advertisement using “fool,” and the ‘sucker’ wording only reached him in July 1892, after his death in 1891. Researcher Ralph Keyes is quoted there saying no modern historian “takes seriously the routine attribution of this slogan to P. T. Barnum.”

A 41-page pamphlet, The Life of Hungry Joe: King of the Bunco Men, says it was always a saying with Joe that there was a sucker born every minute ↗ — six years after the phrase was already in print with no owner.
A Rockford, Illinois paper of 5 September 1889 called it “Mike McDonald’s celebrated maxim” ↗, a decade after the anonymous Chicago printing.

Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ repeats R. J. Brown’s claim that the banker David Hannum said it of the crowds paying to see Barnum’s plaster replica of the Cardiff Giant. Quote Investigator notes that Hannum — along with George Hull, Joseph Bessimer and Adam Forepaugh — appears only in secondary and tertiary sources, with no dated primary citation behind it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody owns it. As Quote Investigator ↗ concludes, both the “fool” and “sucker” versions began with anonymous attributions and were only later reassigned to prominent people — and of all those names, only Barnum’s stuck.

context.heading: A trade proverb that kept changing owners
lead: Nineteenth-century America ran on confidence games, and the trade had its own proverbs. This is one of them: a working swindler’s observation about the reliable supply of marks, printed in gambling columns and police reports for decades before anyone thought to put a name on it. When The Inter-Ocean ran it in January 1879 the paper put it in quotation marks and hung it on an unnamed “old-timer” — the standard signal that a phrase is already common property.

What happened next is the ordinary life-cycle of a good anonymous saying: it gets attached to whoever is famous for the thing it describes. Within a handful of years the same sentence was credited to a bunco man (1885), to a humorist twenty-one years dead (1888), and to a Chicago gambling boss (1889) — before the greatest showman in America absorbed it for good in 1890 and never gave it back.
context.detailsSummary: How the wording drifted, year by year
detailsBody: 1806 — “there vash von fool born every minute,” in an essay in The European Magazine and London Review, put in the mouth of a fictitious dealer in damaged goods.
1826 — “a new fool is born every day,” quoted as an existing principle in The New-York Evening Post.
1835 — “there is a flat born every minute,” in Bell’s Life in London and Sporting Chronicle; “flat” was the period slang for a dupe.
1877 — “there is a fool born every hour,” ascribed to an unnamed London sharper.
1879 — “there’s a sucker born every minute”: the first ‘sucker’ version, anonymous, in The Inter-Ocean of Chicago.
1885–1892 — the same sentence is handed in turn to Hungry Joe Lewis, Artemus Ward, Mike McDonald and finally P. T. Barnum.
context.pull: The phrase was already inside quotation marks in 1879. The newspaper was repeating slang, not quoting a man.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's chronology: 1806 'there vash von fool born every minute' (European Magazine and London Review); 1826 'a new fool is born every day' (New-York Evening Post); 1835 'there is a flat born every minute' (Bell's Life in London); 1877 'a fool born every hour'; earliest 'sucker' instance in 'Gambling in Chicago', The Inter-Ocean, 2 January 1879, p.5 col.2, credited to an anonymous 'old-timer'; 1885 Hungry Joe Lewis pamphlet; first Artemus Ward credit in 'Geneseo Suckers', The Nunda News (Nunda, NY), 6 October 1888, p.3 col.4, in a jewellery-swindle report; September 1889 Mike McDonald (Rockford, Illinois); earliest Barnum link an October 1890 Chicago Tribune Willoughby & Hill advertisement using 'fool'; first 'sucker' link to Barnum July 1892; Barnum died 1891; QI found no persuasive evidence Barnum said it and quotes Ralph Keyes; Hannum, Hull, Bessimer and Forepaugh appear only in secondary/tertiary sources.

The phrase is commonly attributed to P. T. Barnum though there is no evidence he said it; the David Hannum / Cardiff Giant replica theory; the Oxford Dictionary of American Quotations suggests con man Joseph 'Paper Collar Joe' Bessimer; an 1806 variant in The European Magazine predates Barnum's birth.

Wikiquote lists "There's a sucker born every minute" in the Misattributed section of the P. T. Barnum page and repeats R. J. Brown's assertion that it originated with a banker named David Hannum in reference to Barnum's replica of the Cardiff Giant.

Project Gutenberg ebook #6946 is The Complete Works of Artemus Ward by Charles Farrar Browne (seven parts plus a biographical sketch); a full-text search of the HTML edition returns zero occurrences of 'sucker', 'born every', 'every minute' or 'fool born'.

Internet Archive item: Don C. Seitz, 'Artemus Ward (Charles Farrar Browne): a biography and bibliography', Harper, New York, 1919, 408 pages; a full-text search of its OCR text returns zero occurrences of 'sucker', 'born every' or 'every minute'.

Charles Farrar Browne, pen name Artemus Ward, born 26 April 1834 in Waterford, Maine, died 6 March 1867 of tuberculosis at Southampton, England; befriended Mark Twain in Virginia City, Nevada, and recommended him to New York editors; his books appeared 1862-1869; reburied in Waterford, Maine in 1868.
Wikiquote's Artemus Ward page contains no entry for "There's a sucker born every minute" in any section - not sourced, misattributed, disputed or attributed.
The Inter Ocean was a newspaper published in Chicago, Illinois from 1865 until 1914.
